title: SQL Server & T-SQL
description: Learn to query, join and reconcile data safely, then reason about transactions and query plans through a complete order-and-payment case.
prerequisites: No SQL knowledge required. Comfort with files, rows and columns is helpful.
Access to a local or training SQL Server instance and a query client is needed to execute exercises; reading and quizzes work without one.
outcomes: Explain table grain, types, keys and NULL.
Write joins, aggregates, CTEs and window calculations with checked results.
Use typed parameters, temporary staging and rollback-based practice.
Reason about isolation and execution plans without misleading shortcuts.
Build an order/payment reconciliation that preserves unmatched records.
setup: Use a supported SQL Server training instance with SSMS or sqlcmd. No server is installed or started by this website.

Download setup.sql from this path. Review its comments and connect only to your training instance. A login needs permission to create LearningNotebook if it does not exist; otherwise ask the training administrator to create it.
Run setup.sql in SSMS and keep that query window open. All #LN fixture tables are session-local. In another window run setup.sql again to create a separate fixture.
Examples assume the setup fixture is unchanged. Start a new query window and run setup.sql to reset without modifying another session.
Run snippets or solutions.sql in the same session. GO is a client batch separator. Do not paste GO into an application driver call.
The browser does not execute T-SQL. Expected results were checked arithmetically and the content/schema reviewed; no SQL Server engine execution is claimed.
nextSteps: Implement the capstone with permanent tables in a separately approved training database, adding foreign keys and source-batch uniqueness rules.
Practise two-session concurrency with a trainer-controlled shared table and inspect blocking.
Use a larger representative synthetic dataset to compare actual plans and logical reads.
Extend the report to multiple currencies, refunds and late-arriving events without mixing totals.

lessons.title: 1. Connect to a database and read a result
lessons.takeaway: SQL Server stores the data; a query tool sends instructions to it.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A SQL Server instance is a running database engine. One instance can contain several databases. A database contains objects such as tables; a schema groups named objects inside it. A row records one thing at a defined level of detail, and columns describe its attributes. In this course, one order row represents one order, not one payment or one customer.

T-SQL is Microsoft’s SQL dialect. SELECT retrieves a result; INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change data. SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) is a client, not the engine itself. Installing a query tool alone does not create a running server. Connect to an existing local or training SQL Server instance for these exercises; do not use a work production connection.

The browser displays examples and checks your quiz answers; it does not execute SQL. Read setup.sql, run it in SSMS on your training instance, and keep that query window open. It creates LearningNotebook only if absent and uses session-local #LN tables. Opening a second window creates a different session, so its temporary tables are separate.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: The first statement identifies the database and engine version so a result is attached to a real environment. The second counts our five sample orders. GO in the download is a client batch separator recognised by SSMS and sqlcmd; it is not a T-SQL statement to send through a database API.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Check the connection and database before a query that changes data. Our examples use fixed synthetic data; matching a row count is evidence about this fixture, not proof that a production extract is complete. Closing the session removes its local temporary tables. Reopen setup.sql to get a fresh fixture.

exercise.prompt: After running setup.sql, return each customer identifier and name, ordered by identifier.
exercise.starter: SELECT /* columns */ FROM #LNCustomers ORDER BY /* column */;
exercise.solution: SELECT CustomerId, CustomerName FROM #LNCustomers ORDER BY CustomerId;
checks: Four rows: 1 Ada, 2 Ben, 3 Chen, 4 Dia.
Column names are explicit; ordering is requested.

quiz.question: What makes the #LNOrders data available to your next query?
options: Running setup.sql in the same SQL session
quiz.explanation: Local temporary tables belong to a SQL session. Use the same connection/window after setup.

lessons.title: 2. Choose types, keys and missing-value rules
lessons.takeaway: A schema expresses what each value means and which rows are valid.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Use int for these identifiers, decimal(12,2) for the sample amounts, date for dates without a time, and nvarchar for Unicode names. Decimal has a fixed precision and scale; it is useful when two decimal places are part of the business contract. It does not solve every rounding decision. Avoid float for amounts that must compare exactly to a cent.

A primary key uniquely identifies a row and cannot contain NULL. A foreign key in an ordinary permanent table enforces a relationship to an existing parent key. A CHECK constraint restricts allowed values. A constraint prevents invalid writes; an application-side check alone can be bypassed by another writer. SQL Server does not enforce foreign keys on temporary tables, so our fixture uses explicit validation queries for relationships.

NULL means missing or unknown, not zero and not an empty string. Email is optional in the fixture: Ben and Dia have NULL. Equality with NULL does not produce TRUE, so use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Decide whether an unknown amount should stop a report rather than quietly substituting zero.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: COUNT(*) counts all four customers; COUNT(Email) counts the two known emails. The unassigned payment for OrderId 999 is intentionally allowed in the staging fixture. A production payment table with an enforced foreign key would reject it; an incoming staging table may retain it for investigation.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: A nullable column is a modelling decision, not a convenient default for everything. Define which identifiers are required, whether negative amounts represent refunds, and which currency is being counted. All amounts here are synthetic units in one currency.

exercise.prompt: Find customers whose email is known. Return their names in identifier order.
exercise.starter: SELECT CustomerName FROM #LNCustomers WHERE /* missing-value test */ ORDER BY CustomerId;
exercise.solution: SELECT CustomerName FROM #LNCustomers WHERE Email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY CustomerId;
checks: Ada and Chen, in that order.
The predicate uses IS NOT NULL, not <> NULL.

quiz.question: How many rows does WHERE Email = NULL return in this fixture?
quiz.explanation: The comparison is UNKNOWN, not TRUE. WHERE retains TRUE rows; use IS NULL to select the two missing emails.

lessons.title: 3. Filter, calculate and sort deliberately
lessons.takeaway: A query needs explicit predicates, units and ordering.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: SELECT chooses output columns; FROM identifies input rows; WHERE keeps rows meeting a condition. ORDER BY is the output ordering contract. Without it, a familiar-looking order is not guaranteed. TOP without an ORDER BY does not mean the earliest or largest rows.

Use AND for conditions that must both hold and OR for alternatives; parentheses make mixed expressions unambiguous. Date predicates are easier to reason about as a lower bound inclusive and an upper bound exclusive. This also works when a date column later becomes a timestamp.

A computed column alias is available to ORDER BY, but generally not to WHERE in the same query because of SQL’s logical binding order. Logical order explains name scope; it is not a diagram of the optimizer’s physical execution plan.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Our orders are dated January 1, 2 and 3 of 2026. Filtering before January 3 keeps 101, 102 and 103; adding Amount >= 80 keeps 101 and 103. The ISO unseparated date literal avoids ambiguous regional day/month interpretation.
sections.example:
SELECT OrderId, Amount, Amount * 0.10 AS TenPercent
FROM #LNOrders
WHERE OrderDate >= '20260101' AND OrderDate < '20260103'
  AND Amount >= 80
ORDER BY Amount DESC, OrderId;
-- 101:100.00,10.0000; 103:80.00,8.0000 (display scale can vary)

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: SELECT * is convenient during exploration but makes downstream consumers depend on every future column. Integer arithmetic also matters: 5/2 yields 2, whereas CAST(5 AS decimal(10,2))/2 produces a fractional result. State required rounding at the output boundary.

exercise.prompt: Return the two largest orders, using OrderId as the tie-breaker.
exercise.starter: SELECT TOP (2) OrderId, Amount FROM #LNOrders ORDER BY /* criteria */;
exercise.solution: SELECT TOP (2) OrderId, Amount FROM #LNOrders ORDER BY Amount DESC, OrderId;
checks: Ordering makes TOP meaningful and deterministic for tied amounts.

quiz.question: Which query gives a dependable largest-order result?
options: TOP (1) with ORDER BY Amount DESC, OrderId
quiz.explanation: TOP chooses from the requested order; a unique tie-breaker makes ties predictable.

lessons.title: 4. Join without losing or multiplying records
lessons.takeaway: Before joining, say what one row means on each side.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A customer can have many orders. Joining CustomerId therefore produces one output row per matching order, not one per customer. An INNER JOIN keeps matches. A LEFT JOIN also keeps each left-side row with no match, filling the right-side columns with NULL.

An order can have several payments: order 101 has payments 60 and 40. Joining orders directly to payments repeats the order amount for each payment. Summing those repeated amounts would exaggerate sales. Diagnose a join by checking key uniqueness, match counts and unmatched populations before summing money.

A filter on a right-hand column in WHERE can remove the NULL-extended rows of a LEFT JOIN. Put a right-side eligibility condition in ON when the requirement is to preserve all left rows and attach only qualifying right rows. This is a semantic choice, not a performance trick.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Dia has no order. LEFT JOIN preserves her as one row with a NULL OrderId. Customers 1 and 2 each appear twice; customer 3 once; customer 4 once, so the output has six rows.
sections.example:
SELECT c.CustomerId, c.CustomerName, o.OrderId
FROM #LNCustomers AS c
LEFT JOIN #LNOrders AS o ON o.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
ORDER BY c.CustomerId, o.OrderId;
-- 1/101,1/102,2/103,2/104,3/105,4/NULL

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: DISTINCT is not a repair for an unexplained join expansion. It can hide duplicate evidence or discard legitimate repeated values. If the desired grain is one row per order, aggregate payments to that grain before joining; the next lesson builds that stage.

exercise.prompt: Find customers with no orders. Use an anti-match and return identifier/name.
checks: Only 4/Dia.
A LEFT JOIN with WHERE o.OrderId IS NULL is also correct.

quiz.question: Order 101 has two payment rows. What happens to its 100 order amount in a direct join?
options: It appears on both joined rows
quiz.explanation: Joining attaches matching rows; it does not allocate the order amount across them. Summing it now double counts.

lessons.title: 5. Aggregate at a stated grain
lessons.takeaway: GROUP BY collapses rows; WHERE and HAVING filter different stages.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Grouping by CustomerId returns one row per customer represented in the orders. SUM adds amounts; COUNT(*) counts rows; AVG calculates a mean of non-NULL values. Aggregates generally ignore NULL values, while COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of column values. An absent group is different from a group whose known amounts sum to zero.

WHERE limits input rows before grouping. HAVING limits groups after aggregate values exist. To count a customer’s orders after a LEFT JOIN, COUNT(o.OrderId) counts the matched non-NULL identifiers; COUNT(*) would count the placeholder row for a customer with no order.

Always label the denominator: average order value is total amount divided by order count, not by customer count. A mean of customer means is not the overall order mean unless the weights happen to match.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Customer 1 has 150 across two orders; customer 2 has 200 across two; customer 3 has 40 across one. The totals reconcile to 390 and five orders. A HAVING threshold of 150 includes 1 and 2.
sections.example:
SELECT CustomerId, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount, SUM(Amount) AS Total
FROM #LNOrders
GROUP BY CustomerId
HAVING SUM(Amount) >= 150
ORDER BY CustomerId;
-- 1,2,150.00; 2,2,200.00

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: A report that excludes customers with no orders may be fine for sales totals but wrong for customer coverage. Start from the customer table when that population must be preserved, and make the no-order policy explicit.

exercise.prompt: Return all four customers with order counts, including zero for Dia.
checks: Counts sum to 5; customer population stays 4.

quiz.question: Which clause filters a grouped customer total greater than 100?
quiz.explanation: HAVING filters grouped results. WHERE is for the rows supplied to the grouping operation.

lessons.title: 6. Use CTEs and subqueries to name intermediate ideas
lessons.takeaway: A named query step improves reasoning; it is not automatically a stored result.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A subquery is a query inside another statement. EXISTS asks whether at least one matching row exists without multiplying the outer row. A common table expression (CTE) names a result within the next statement, so a long transformation can be read in stages.

A CTE is scoped to that one following statement. It is not a permanent table or a guaranteed performance cache. Prefix WITH with a semicolon when a preceding statement might lack its terminator. Multiple CTEs in one WITH are separated by commas.
For this report, first reduce payments to one row per OrderId, then attach that total to the orders. This changes the grain before the join so a two-payment order no longer duplicates its amount.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Order 104 has no payment total and is NULL after the join. COALESCE turns that absence into zero only for this specific amount calculation; retain a separate missing-payment indicator when it matters to the workflow.
sections.example:
;WITH Paid AS (
 SELECT OrderId, SUM(Amount) AS PaidAmount FROM #LNPayments GROUP BY OrderId
)
SELECT o.OrderId, o.Amount, COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS PaidAmount
FROM #LNOrders o LEFT JOIN Paid p ON p.OrderId=o.OrderId
ORDER BY o.OrderId;
-- 101:100;102:50;103:70;104:0;105:45 paid

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: NOT IN against a list containing NULL can unexpectedly reject rows because of UNKNOWN comparisons. NOT EXISTS with an explicit equality is usually a clearer expression for unmatched keys. Never discard unknown keys before recording their exception count.

exercise.prompt: Use NOT EXISTS to find incoming payments with an unknown OrderId.
exercise.starter:
SELECT p.PaymentId,p.OrderId,p.Amount FROM #LNPayments p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (/* correlated order lookup */);
checks: 206,999,20.00 is the single orphan.
The unknown payment is reported, not silently joined away.

quiz.question: Can a CTE name be reused by an unrelated second SELECT statement?
options: No, its scope is the next statement
quiz.explanation: A CTE names a query expression for one statement. Use a temporary table when a later statement needs stored intermediate rows.

lessons.title: 7. Rank rows and compute running totals
lessons.takeaway: A window calculation retains detail rows while looking across related rows.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: GROUP BY collapses a group to fewer rows. A window function uses OVER to calculate across a related set while keeping each original row. PARTITION BY starts a separate window per customer; ORDER BY defines sequence within it.

ROW_NUMBER assigns sequential numbers. To select the latest order reliably, order by OrderDate descending and then OrderId descending. The identifier resolves same-date ties. RANK and DENSE_RANK treat ties differently, so select a function to match the business question rather than because its name sounds right.

For a running sum, explicitly use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. That means every preceding row plus this one in the specified order. The outer query still needs ORDER BY to control display order.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Ben’s two orders occur on January 2 and 3, so his running total is 80 then 200. Ada’s is 100 then 150; Chen’s is 40. The result still has five order rows.
sections.example:
SELECT CustomerId, OrderId, Amount,
 SUM(Amount) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate,OrderId
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS RunningTotal
FROM #LNOrders ORDER BY CustomerId,OrderDate,OrderId;

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: ROW_NUMBER is not a stored primary key. It can change when the input changes. For latest-row selection, rank in a CTE and filter rn=1 outside it; the alias cannot be filtered in WHERE in that same SELECT.

exercise.prompt: Return the latest order for each customer who has orders.
exercise.starter:
;WITH Ranked AS (SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY /* latest */) AS rn FROM #LNOrders)
SELECT CustomerId,OrderId FROM Ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY CustomerId;
exercise.solution:
;WITH Ranked AS (SELECT CustomerId,OrderId,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId ORDER BY OrderDate DESC,OrderId DESC) AS rn FROM #LNOrders)
SELECT CustomerId,OrderId FROM Ranked WHERE rn=1 ORDER BY CustomerId;
checks: Dia is absent because she has no order; include her only through a separate population join.

quiz.question: Why add OrderId after OrderDate to the ranking order?
quiz.explanation: A unique tie-breaker prevents equal dates from leaving the selected latest row ambiguous.

lessons.title: 8. Use parameters and stored procedures
lessons.takeaway: Pass data as typed parameters; keep SQL text separate from values.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A parameter is a named input with a declared SQL type. Parameters make the value contract explicit and avoid building SQL by concatenating user text. Applications should bind parameters through their database driver. Parameterization helps prevent value-based SQL injection; it is not a replacement for access control or input validation.

A stored procedure is a named database program invoked with EXEC. It can contain queries and control flow. SET NOCOUNT ON suppresses row-count messages, not the query result. The lesson example creates a local temporary procedure, so it disappears when this SQL session ends and changes no permanent application code.

In SSMS, CREATE PROCEDURE belongs in its own batch. The GO separators below are important. The procedure relies on the caller’s temporary fixture only for this lesson; a deployed procedure normally uses explicitly qualified permanent tables with a designed permission model.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Requesting CustomerId 2 produces orders 103 and 104. Calling the same procedure for 4 gives an empty result because Dia has no orders. That is a legitimate result, not a SQL exception.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Identifiers such as table names cannot be supplied as ordinary value parameters. If identifiers must vary, use a controlled allowlist and appropriate quoting. Do not concatenate them from arbitrary input. Different parameter values can also have different selectivity: reusing a plan is not a guarantee of good performance.

exercise.prompt: Use sp_executesql with a typed parameter to return orders with amounts at least 90; do not concatenate 90 into the SQL text.
exercise.starter: EXEC sys.sp_executesql N'SELECT OrderId,Amount FROM #LNOrders WHERE Amount>=@Minimum ORDER BY OrderId;', /* type declaration */, /* value */;
exercise.solution: EXEC sys.sp_executesql N'SELECT OrderId,Amount FROM #LNOrders WHERE Amount>=@Minimum ORDER BY OrderId;', N'@Minimum decimal(12,2)', @Minimum=90;
checks: @Minimum is declared and supplied separately from statement text.

quiz.question: What should an application do with a user-supplied minimum amount?
options: Bind it as a typed parameter
quiz.explanation: Typed parameters separate values from executable SQL text. Validate business limits and use least-privilege permissions as well.

lessons.title: 9. Stage work and practise safe data changes
lessons.takeaway: Temporary tables store intermediate rows; changes still need a clear scope.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: A # temporary table exists in tempdb with session-local visibility. Unlike a CTE, it can be reused by later statements and can have indexes. It consumes resources and is not automatically faster; choose it when inspecting, indexing or reusing an intermediate result helps.

INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes matching rows, and DELETE removes matching rows. A missing WHERE on an UPDATE or DELETE affects every row. For practice, we change a dedicated #LNWork copy rather than the base fixture, and put the demonstration inside a transaction that rolls back.

SELECT INTO creates a new table from query output. It does not mean every constraint and index from the source has been reproduced. For a controlled production staging design, CREATE TABLE first and explicitly INSERT the selected columns.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: The script copies five orders, adds 10 to order 103, observes 90, then rolls back to 80. The copied table exists before BEGIN TRAN, so it remains after rollback. Rerunning this example replaces only the session-local work copy.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Record @@ROWCOUNT immediately after the relevant modification: subsequent statements can replace it. A targeted update that affects zero rows may indicate a missing identifier or concurrency conflict. Inspect it rather than claiming success because no exception occurred.

exercise.prompt: Copy orders to #LNExerciseWork and delete only order 105 inside a transaction. Show the row count before rollback; then prove all five rows remain.
exercise.starter: -- Create a temporary work copy, BEGIN TRAN, DELETE with WHERE, inspect @@ROWCOUNT, ROLLBACK.
checks: DeletedRows=1; RemainingRows=5.
The original #LNOrders still contains all five rows.

quiz.question: When should you capture @@ROWCOUNT after an UPDATE?
quiz.explanation: @@ROWCOUNT describes the previous relevant statement and can be reset by subsequent statements.

lessons.title: 10. Make a unit of work atomic and consider concurrency
lessons.takeaway: A transaction groups changes; isolation determines what concurrent sessions can observe.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: BEGIN TRAN starts an explicit transaction; COMMIT completes it; ROLLBACK undoes its transactional changes. Atomicity means the unit succeeds together or is undone. Keep transactions short and avoid waiting for a person while locks are held. A client disconnect or timeout is not a substitute for a designed error-handling strategy.

TRY/CATCH lets this example roll back when a statement fails. SET XACT_ABORT ON makes many runtime errors terminate and roll back the transaction. In CATCH, XACT_STATE reports whether a transaction remains and whether it is committable; THROW propagates the original error.

Isolation is about overlapping sessions. READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads, but a later statement can see newly committed changes. Its implementation depends on the database’s READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT setting. SNAPSHOT needs database configuration and gives a transaction-level versioned view; SERIALIZABLE protects ranges more strongly and can increase blocking. NOLOCK permits unreliable reads and is unsuitable as a reconciliation fix.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: This deliberately throws after an update to a work copy. The CATCH rolls it back and returns an explanatory result instead of rethrowing, solely so the final verification runs. A real application should usually propagate the failure. Starting an outer transaction beforehand would change rollback scope; run the exercise with @@TRANCOUNT=0.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Single-session temporary tables cannot demonstrate inter-session blocking because other sessions cannot access them. For a later concurrency lab, have a trainer supply a dedicated shared table and a two-session script. Do not change isolation database options on a shared database just to make an example run.

exercise.prompt: Inspect this database’s row-versioning settings without changing them. Explain why the result matters for READ COMMITTED.
exercise.starter: SELECT name, /* row versioning flags */ FROM sys.databases WHERE name=DB_NAME();
checks: One row for LearningNotebook; exact flag values depend on setup and are not assumed.
Explain statement-level versioning when READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is enabled.

quiz.question: Does READ COMMITTED guarantee two SELECT statements see identical data?
options: No, another transaction may commit between them
quiz.explanation: Avoiding dirty reads is different from holding a stable view across multiple statements.

lessons.title: 11. Read a plan before tuning a query
lessons.takeaway: Indexes trade read access paths against storage and write costs.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: An index is an additional access structure the optimizer may use. A clustered rowstore index organizes the table’s rows by its key; a nonclustered index provides another ordered access path with a row locator. An INCLUDE column can cover output without being part of the search key. More indexes also mean more maintenance during writes.

An execution plan shows chosen operators such as scans, seeks, sorts and joins. Estimated plans show predictions; actual plans add runtime information. Compare estimated and actual row counts, warnings and expensive work, not only the largest percentage label. A seek is not automatically good and a scan is not automatically bad.

A predicate such as OrderDate >= @From AND OrderDate < @To can support an index range access more naturally than wrapping OrderDate in YEAR(). Whether an index is chosen still depends on data volume, distribution, statistics and required output. Our five-row fixture is too small to establish performance gains.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Create an index on a temporary copy, enable statistics, and inspect the actual plan in SSMS. The returned values must stay unchanged. With five rows the optimizer may prefer a scan, and either elapsed time can round to zero: this is a plan-reading exercise.

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: Do not add every suggested missing index or force a join hint without a representative workload. A fast query that drops unmatched records is still wrong. First freeze the correctness checks, then compare evidence on data and parameters representative of actual use.

exercise.prompt: Rewrite YEAR(OrderDate)=2026 as a range predicate. Return only OrderId and verify all five identifiers.
exercise.starter: SELECT OrderId FROM #LNOrders WHERE /* half-open date range */ ORDER BY OrderId;
exercise.solution: SELECT OrderId FROM #LNOrders WHERE OrderDate>='20260101' AND OrderDate<'20270101' ORDER BY OrderId;
checks: No function is applied to OrderDate; no speed improvement is claimed from this tiny fixture.

quiz.question: What should you conclude if the five-row table still uses a scan after adding an index?
options: A scan may be the sensible plan at this size
quiz.explanation: Plan quality depends on the cost of the whole operation and the data; operator names alone do not establish performance.

lessons.title: 12. Build an order-to-payment reconciliation
lessons.takeaway: A trustworthy report preserves populations, reconciles totals and exposes exceptions.

sections.title: Understand the idea
paragraphs: Your stakeholder wants to know which orders are paid. Define the grain as one row per order, the scope as all five fixture orders, and the matching rule as OrderId. All amounts share one currency. Payment rows are staging observations: an unknown order is an exception to report, not evidence that an order should be invented.

First aggregate the six payment rows by OrderId. Then left join the five orders to that result. Keep missing payment evidence separate from a known total of zero, and calculate outstanding as amount due minus matched payments. A negative outstanding amount means overpayment in this teaching contract.

The report has two outputs: five order rows and an orphan-payment list. A grand-total subtraction of 390-285=105 is misleading for order balances because 20 of incoming payments belongs to unknown OrderId 999. Matched payments total 265, leaving net outstanding 125. Positive outstanding is 130; overpayment is 5; net 130-5=125.

sections.title: Walk through an example
paragraphs: Expected order statuses:101 paid,102 paid,103 underpaid by 10,104 missing with 120 outstanding,105 overpaid by 5. The orphan list contains 206/999/20. Check both row counts and values; a result containing the right total but duplicated rows is not acceptable.
sections.example:
;WITH Paid AS (
 SELECT OrderId,COUNT(*) AS PaymentCount,SUM(Amount) AS PaidAmount
 FROM #LNPayments GROUP BY OrderId
)
SELECT o.OrderId,o.Amount AS Due,COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Paid,
 o.Amount-COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Outstanding,
 CASE WHEN p.OrderId IS NULL THEN 'missing'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount=o.Amount THEN 'paid'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount<o.Amount THEN 'underpaid'
      ELSE 'overpaid' END AS Status
FROM #LNOrders o LEFT JOIN Paid p ON p.OrderId=o.OrderId
ORDER BY o.OrderId;
SELECT p.PaymentId,p.OrderId,p.Amount FROM #LNPayments p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM #LNOrders o WHERE o.OrderId=p.OrderId)
ORDER BY p.PaymentId;

sections.title: Common mistake and better habit
paragraphs: A rerun must not append duplicate logical exceptions. A real pipeline needs source batch identifiers, source-row keys, duplicate policy, currency, effective time and approval rules. This capstone produces read-only results, so repeated execution does not post transactions. Duplicated PaymentId rows would be rejected by the fixture primary key; duplicate business events with different identifiers still require a separate policy.

exercise.prompt: Write the two report outputs without looking at the solution. Explain why the orphan 20 is excluded from matched paid totals. Then describe how a duplicate payment event would change your design.
exercise.starter:
-- 1 Aggregate payments by OrderId.
-- 2 LEFT JOIN to the order population.
-- 3 CASE classify missing/paid/underpaid/overpaid.
-- 4 NOT EXISTS for orphan payments.
exercise.solution:
;WITH Paid AS (
 SELECT OrderId,COUNT(*) AS PaymentCount,SUM(Amount) AS PaidAmount
 FROM #LNPayments GROUP BY OrderId
)
SELECT o.OrderId,o.Amount AS Due,COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Paid,
 o.Amount-COALESCE(p.PaidAmount,0) AS Outstanding,
 CASE WHEN p.OrderId IS NULL THEN 'missing'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount=o.Amount THEN 'paid'
      WHEN p.PaidAmount<o.Amount THEN 'underpaid'
      ELSE 'overpaid' END AS Status
FROM #LNOrders o LEFT JOIN Paid p ON p.OrderId=o.OrderId
ORDER BY o.OrderId;
SELECT p.PaymentId,p.OrderId,p.Amount FROM #LNPayments p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM #LNOrders o WHERE o.OrderId=p.OrderId)
ORDER BY p.PaymentId;
checks: Exactly 5 order rows and 1 orphan row.
Due 390, matched paid 265, net outstanding 125.
Status counts:paid 2,underpaid 1,missing 1,overpaid 1.
All payment amounts 285 = matched 265 + orphan 20.
A duplicate-event policy is described without silently using DISTINCT on monetary values.

quiz.question: Why is 390 minus 285 not the correct net outstanding for known orders?
options: The 285 includes 20 assigned to an unknown order
All payment rows should be removed
quiz.explanation: Only 265 is matched to known orders. Preserve the remaining 20 as an orphan exception instead of using it to reduce known balances.
